item.title: How Force Merge Compaction Nearly Doubled Milvus Search QPS
item.content:encoded:
I recently found myself wrestling with a semantic search service that was performing adequately, but not optimally. We had ingested a substantial corpus of documents, and while initial QPS numbers were acceptable, I suspected there was headroom being left on the table. My intuition, honed from years of working with traditional database storage engines, pointed to the underlying segment structure. Specifically, I wondered if the proliferation of small, sealed segments, a common pattern in systems like Milvus after bulk ingestion, was introducing unnecessary overhead. Every query, I reasoned, would have to fan out across these numerous segments, incurring costs for scheduling, index lookups, and result merging that could potentially be avoided.

My thesis was straightforward: consolidating these small segments into fewer, larger ones should reduce query fan-out and, consequently, improve QPS. The question was, by how much? And what would be the cost of such an operation? This led me to investigate Milvus’s compact() API, and specifically, the target_size option for what it calls "Force Merge Compaction."

Why Small Segments Accumulate

Before diving into the solution, it’s important to understand the problem. Why does Milvus, or any similar system, end up with many small segments in the first place?

The core reason is that the system cannot inherently know when your write workload is complete. Imagine a continuous stream of data, or a series of incremental updates and deletes. Each of these operations, or periodic flushes, can result in a new sealed segment. Merging these segments isn’t free; it consumes I/O, memory, and CPU, and often requires rebuilding the index for the newly merged data. If the system were to aggressively merge segments while writes were still ongoing, it would waste resources and potentially impact write throughput and stability. So, the safe default is to leave sealed segments alone.

This leads to an accumulation of segments over time. While this layout is perfectly valid for data integrity, it’s often not the most performant for query serving, especially in read-heavy scenarios. The system prioritizes write stability and availability, leaving the optimization for read performance to the operator.

This is where the operator’s knowledge becomes crucial. The system doesn’t know that a bulk import has just finished, or that a knowledge base refresh is complete, or that a collection has transitioned from a write-heavy phase to a read-heavy one. Force Merge is the mechanism by which we, as engineers, signal this change in workload pattern to the system, trading a one-time reorganization cost for long-term query performance gains.

How Force Merge Compaction Works

Force Merge Compaction in Milvus is designed to address this segment fragmentation. It consolidates many small, scattered segments into a smaller number of larger ones, with a target size that can be specified. It’s invoked via the existing compact() API, but with the addition of a target_size parameter.

What makes Force Merge different from standard compaction is its ability to:

  1. Merge many-to-many: Unlike standard compaction, which typically merges a few small segments into slightly larger ones, Force Merge can regroup numerous segments into output segments that are closer to the desired target_size.
  2. Bypass the per-segment size cap: Standard compaction adheres strictly to a dataCoord.segment.maxSize limit. Once segments reach a size where merging two would exceed this cap, standard compaction stops. Force Merge, however, can exceed this cap, allowing for more aggressive consolidation.

Let me walk through how this actually works. Consider a scenario with five 2MB segments and a maxSize of 3MB. Standard compaction wouldn't be able to merge any two segments, as that would result in a 4MB segment, exceeding the 3MB limit. The segment count would remain at five. With Force Merge, if I specify a target_size of 4MB, it can collapse those five 2MB segments into fewer, larger segments, even if they exceed the maxSize for individual segments under normal operation.

The interesting thing here is the impact on graph indexes like HNSW. For HNSW, the search cost for a single, larger segment does not increase proportionally to its size. This means that reducing the number of segments from, say, three to one, is a net win. You’re not just moving the cost around; you’re eliminating the overhead associated with managing and querying multiple independent indexes.

Force Merge also operates asynchronously, meaning it runs in the background without blocking ongoing search or query operations. However, it does consume I/O, memory, and CPU resources during its execution, particularly during the index rebuild phase for the new, larger segments. This is a critical trade-off to consider.

The target_size parameter itself offers three modes:

  • Omitted or 0: This behaves like standard compaction, respecting the maxSize configuration.
  • Explicit size in MB: You specify a target size (e.g., 1024 for 1GB). This value must be greater than or equal to the configured maxSize; otherwise, it will be rejected.
  • max_int64: This is an auto mode where Milvus determines the optimal target size based on the current segment layout and the memory available to the QueryNodes, ensuring the merged segments remain loadable. This auto mode is generally recommended unless you have a very specific sizing requirement.

Experiment Setup: Isolating Segment Shape

My hypothesis was that fewer segments would lead to less query fan-out, and less fan-out would translate to higher QPS. To validate this, I designed a controlled experiment. The goal was to isolate the impact of segment shape, meaning all other variables — dataset, index type, query load, and concurrency levels — were kept constant across two runs.

Here’s the setup I used:

The process involved:

  1. Ingesting 1 million 768-dimensional vectors.
  2. Allowing segments to seal.
  3. Running a baseline QPS benchmark.
  4. Applying Force Merge Compaction.
  5. Running a second QPS benchmark.

Baseline: Three Sealed Segments, ~3,000 QPS

For the baseline run, I deliberately skipped Force Merge. After ingesting 1 million vectors, I observed in Attu (Milvus’s GUI) that the collection had settled into three sealed segments, each holding approximately 300,000+ rows. Once the HNSW index finished building on these segments, I initiated the concurrency sweep.

What I found was that QPS plateaued around 3,000, even as I increased the concurrency levels from 80 up to 240. My Grafana dashboards showed that the Milvus server’s CPU was consistently pinned during the query phase. At higher concurrency levels, the load generator also started to show signs of bottlenecking.

This observation was critical: the performance ceiling was clearly in the search execution path, specifically in how it utilized CPU resources, rather than in network or disk I/O. This immediately raised the question: could reducing the segment count free up some of that CPU headroom?

After Force Merge: One Segment, ~5,600–6,000 QPS

For the second run, I introduced Force Merge. After the initial data ingestion and sealing of segments, I executed a compact() call with target_size=max_int64. This initiated the asynchronous merge process.

from pymilvus import Collection

# Assuming 'my_collection' is an existing Collection object
# And 'my_collection_name' is the name of the collection

# Trigger Force Merge Compaction with auto-sizing
# In a real scenario, you'd likely want to monitor the compaction status
# This is a simplified example.
try:
    collection = Collection("my_collection_name")
    collection.compact(target_size=2**63 - 1) # max_int64
    print(f"Force Merge Compaction initiated for collection '{my_collection_name}'.")
    print("Monitor Milvus logs and Attu for completion and segment status.")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error initiating compaction: {e}")

After the compaction completed, the three original 300,000-row segments had been consolidated into a single segment containing all 1 million rows. Milvus then rebuilt the HNSW index for this new, larger segment. During this index rebuild, I observed the 16 cores of my virtual machine being fully utilized. This was the trade-off in plain sight: Force Merge incurs its cost upfront, during the merge and index rebuild, but aims to pay it back later in the query phase. In a distributed environment, one could potentially isolate these costs by using separate DataNode and QueryNode resources, or leverage GPU acceleration for index building. On my single-node setup, the rebuild competed directly for CPU and I/O.

Once the new, consolidated segment was indexed, I re-ran the same concurrency sweep. The results were stark. The baseline QPS, which hovered around 3,000, jumped to approximately 5,600 to 6,000 after Force Merge. At 120 concurrency, it reached about 5,600 QPS; at 160 and 200, it was closer to 5,700–5,800 QPS. Both Grafana and the VDBBench summary confirmed this significant improvement.

The p99 latency also saw a substantial reduction, dropping by roughly a third across most concurrency levels. This gap between the baseline and post-merge performance visually represented the “fan-out tax.” With one segment instead of three, each query no longer had to pay for redundant searches, scheduling, and result merging. The CPU cycles previously consumed by this overhead were now available to serve more queries, nearly doubling the QPS.

It’s worth noting the 240-concurrency row. Both baseline and Force Merge QPS numbers dropped there (to 2,303 and 4,311 respectively). This was because my 32-core load generator, not Milvus, became the bottleneck. However, the percentage improvement, at +87%, still held, indicating the underlying efficiency gain.

When to Use Force Merge (and When Not To)

Based on these experiments, it’s clear that Force Merge is not a universal solution. It’s a powerful tool when applied judiciously.

The key takeaway is that Force Merge is a maintenance action. It’s designed for collections where the data has largely settled and the workload has shifted to being read-heavy. The cost of the merge and index rebuild is a one-time expenditure that is recouped through sustained higher query throughput and lower latency.

In my experiments, consolidating 1 million 768-dimensional vectors with an HNSW graph index on a single-node Docker Compose setup nearly doubled QPS, from approximately 3,000 to 5,600–6,000. This isn’t a reason to apply Force Merge everywhere, but for static, read-heavy collections with fragmented segments, segment shape is a critical performance variable that warrants direct measurement and optimization.

Force Merge runs asynchronously and won’t block queries, but it does consume I/O and memory, and can temporarily raise query latency during the index rebuild phase. Therefore, I strongly recommend running it during a quiet window and carefully monitoring the segment count and system resources before and after. Treat it as a maintenance action that you can observe, roll back if necessary, and re-run. Prove the gain on your specific data and workload first, then determine if it earns a place in your operational routine.

item.title: Postgres Index Types Explained: B-tree, GIN, BRIN, and Operators
item.content:encoded:
In my post about JSON and JSONB I told you to create a GIN index with jsonb_path_ops and moved on, because that post was about a column type and not about indexing. This one pays the debt. What a GIN index actually is, why Postgres ships five other index types.

Every example below runs as written on a stock Postgres 17. The plans and sizes are real output from my machine.

An index is a bet

An index is a separate data structure that trades write speed and disk for read speed. Every insert and update has to maintain every index on the table, and every index occupies real space, which you will see measured at the end of this post. That framing matters because the question is never “should I index this table” but “which reads are worth taxing my writes for”. An index that no query uses is a pure tax.

Indexes accelerate operators, not columns

When the planner considers an index, it does not ask “is there an index on this column”. It asks “is there an index whose type knows how to answer this operator”. A B-tree knows how to answer =, <, <=, >=, > and BETWEEN, because it keeps values in sorted order. It has no idea what to do with the array containment operator @>. A GIN index answers @> natively and cannot help you with <.

The glue between an index type and the operators it serves is called an operator class. Most of the time the default class is what you want and you never type its name. The moment it becomes practical is when one index type offers a choice, which is exactly the jsonb_ops versus jsonb_path_ops decision from the JSONB post: same GIN machinery, different set of supported operators, different size.

Keep that lens for the rest of the post. Each index type below is just a different answer to the question “which operators do you need to be fast”.

The demo table

One table, one million rows, shaped like an event log because that is where indexing decisions get interesting: a user id to look up, a status that is almost always ok, a tags array, and a timestamp that grows with insert order.

CREATE TABLE events (
  id         bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id    int    NOT NULL,
  status     text   NOT NULL,
  tags       text[] NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO events (user_id, status, tags, created_at)
SELECT
  i % 50000,
  CASE WHEN i % 211 = 0 THEN 'failed' ELSE 'ok' END,
  ARRAY['app' || i % 7, (ARRAY['auth', 'billing', 'search', 'export', 'sync'])[1 + i % 5]]
    || CASE WHEN i % 397 = 0 THEN ARRAY['beta'] ELSE '{}' END,
  timestamptz '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' + i * interval '2 seconds'
FROM generate_series(0, 999999) AS i;

ANALYZE events;

Life without an index

Ask for one user’s events with nothing but the primary key in place:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 12345;
Gather (actual rows=20 loops=1)
   Workers Planned: 2
   Workers Launched: 2
   ->  Parallel Seq Scan on events (actual rows=7 loops=3)
         Filter: (user_id = 12345)
         Rows Removed by Filter: 333327
 Planning Time: 0.083 ms
 Execution Time: 15.696 ms

Postgres read the entire table and threw two parallel workers at it to make that less painful. Twenty matching rows required inspecting a million. A sequential scan is the baseline, and on small tables it is often the genuinely fastest plan. On a million rows, for twenty matches, it is the thing indexes exist to avoid.

B-tree, the default for a reason

CREATE INDEX with no USING clause gives you a B-tree, a balanced tree of sorted values. Sorted order is why it covers the widest set of operators: equality, every comparison, BETWEEN, and it can feed ORDER BY without a sort step.

CREATE INDEX events_user_id_idx ON events (user_id);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 12345;
Bitmap Heap Scan on events (actual rows=20 loops=1)
   Recheck Cond: (user_id = 12345)
   Heap Blocks: exact=20
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_user_id_idx (actual rows=20 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (user_id = 12345)
 Planning Time: 0.087 ms
 Execution Time: 0.046 ms

From 15.7 milliseconds to 0.046. Same query, same data, three hundred times faster.

A bitmap scan is a two-phase strategy. The Bitmap Index Scan walks the index and collects the locations of every matching row into a bitmap in memory. The Bitmap Heap Scan then sorts those locations by page and visits each table page exactly once. When matches are scattered across the table, as they are here, this beats jumping back and forth between index and table row by row. You will meet this plan shape with every index type in this post, because GIN and BRIN produce their results as bitmaps by nature.

The same B-tree serves range queries for free:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id BETWEEN 100 AND 199;
Bitmap Heap Scan on events (actual rows=2000 loops=1)
   Recheck Cond: ((user_id >= 100) AND (user_id <= 199))
   Heap Blocks: exact=41
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_user_id_idx (actual rows=2000 loops=1)
         Index Cond: ((user_id >= 100) AND (user_id <= 199))
 Planning Time: 0.048 ms
 Execution Time: 0.137 ms

If your predicate is equality or ordering on a scalar, the B-tree is almost always the answer, which is why it is the default.

GIN, the inverted index

A B-tree stores one entry per row. That model collapses when a single value contains many searchable elements: an array of tags, the keys of a jsonb document, the words of a text document. You do not want an entry per row, you want an entry per element, pointing back at every row containing it. That structure is an inverted index, and in Postgres it is called GIN, for Generalized Inverted Index.

CREATE INDEX events_tags_idx ON events USING gin (tags);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT * FROM events WHERE tags @> ARRAY['beta'];
Bitmap Heap Scan on events (actual rows=2519 loops=1)
   Recheck Cond: (tags @> '{beta}'::text[])
   Heap Blocks: exact=2519
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_tags_idx (actual rows=2519 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (tags @> '{beta}'::text[])
 Planning Time: 0.105 ms
 Execution Time: 1.712 ms

The @> containment operator asks "does this array contain these elements", the GIN index looks up beta in its element catalog, and 2,519 rows come back without touching the other 997,481. Swap the array for a jsonb column and this is exactly the index and operator pair from the JSONB post. Full-text search runs on the same machinery.

The cost side: GIN is the most expensive index here to maintain on writes, because one row insert may add many index entries. It earns that cost only when your queries genuinely ask containment-style questions.

BRIN, the index that is barely there

BRIN, Block Range Index, does not store row locations at all. It stores a summary per range of table pages, by default the minimum and maximum value found in each range of 128 pages. A query for a value range lets Postgres skip every block range whose summary cannot contain a match.

That only works when the physical layout correlates with the values, which is precisely the situation of a timestamp on an append-only table: rows arrive in time order, so each block range covers a narrow slice of time.

CREATE INDEX events_created_brin ON events USING brin (created_at);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM events
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-10' AND created_at < '2026-01-11';
Aggregate (actual rows=1 loops=1)
   ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on events (actual rows=43200 loops=1)
         Recheck Cond: ((created_at >= '2026-01-10 00:00:00+00'...))
         Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 13120
         Heap Blocks: lossy=640
         ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_created_brin (actual rows=6400 loops=1)
               Index Cond: (...)
 Planning Time: 0.093 ms
 Execution Time: 3.755 ms

Note lossy=640 and the recheck removing 13,120 rows. BRIN cannot say "row 5 matches", only "something in these pages might match", so Postgres visits the candidate pages and filters. That imprecision is the price of the headline number:

CREATE INDEX events_created_btree ON events (created_at);

SELECT relname AS index_name, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid)) AS size
FROM pg_class
WHERE relname IN ('events_created_brin', 'events_created_btree');
index_name      | size
----------------------+-------
 events_created_brin  | 24 kB
 events_created_btree | 21 MB

Twenty-four kilobytes against twenty-one megabytes for the same column, a factor of nearly a thousand. On logging, metrics, and event tables that only grow, BRIN buys you most of the benefit for a rounding error of disk and near-zero write overhead. On columns with no physical correlation it buys you nothing, which is the trade in one sentence.

Partial and expression indexes

These are not index types but modifiers that apply to any of the above, and they solve extremely common problems.

A partial index carries a WHERE clause and only indexes matching rows. My status column is failed in less than half a percent of rows, and failed rows are the only ones I ever look up by status:

CREATE INDEX events_failed_idx ON events (created_at) WHERE status = 'failed';

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT * FROM events
WHERE status = 'failed' AND created_at >= '2026-01-20';
Index Scan using events_failed_idx on events (actual rows=849 loops=1)
   Index Cond: (created_at >= '2026-01-20 00:00:00+00'...)
 Planning Time: 0.226 ms
 Execution Time: 0.515 ms

The index is 120 kB against 21 MB for its full-table equivalent, and every insert of an ok row skips it entirely. This plan is also a plain Index Scan rather than a bitmap: few enough rows, so Postgres walks the index and fetches rows directly.

An expression index indexes the result of an expression instead of a raw column, which is how you index lower(email), or a single hot key extracted from a jsonb document:

CREATE INDEX chunks_source_type_idx ON chunks ((metadata ->> 'source_type'));

That line is lifted directly from the JSONB post, and it is worth restating what it does: it gives one JSON key an ordinary B-tree with ordinary statistics, no GIN involved.

The bill

Everything above, measured. This is the table and every index this post created on it:

relname               |    size
----------------------+------------
 events               | 89 MB
 events_pkey          | 21 MB
 events_created_btree | 21 MB
 events_user_id_idx   | 7600 kB
 events_tags_idx      | 2360 kB
 events_failed_idx    | 120 kB
 events_created_brin  | 24 kB

The indexes together add up to more than half the size of the table itself, and every row written pays maintenance on all of them. This is why “just add an index” is not free advice, and why the sizes span three orders of magnitude for the same job on the same data.

Let the operator choose

After all of this, the decision procedure is short, because the operator in your WHERE clause has already made it. Equality and ranges on scalars want a B-tree. Containment questions against arrays, jsonb, or text search want GIN. Time ranges over huge append-only tables want BRIN. Then partial and expression modifiers narrow whichever one you picked to the rows and expressions you actually query.

When a plan surprises you, read it with the operator lens: EXPLAIN ANALYZE tells you which index answered which condition, and a sequential scan usually means no index on the table speaks the operator you used, or the table is small enough that speaking it does not matter.

If the GIN line in my JSONB post sent you here, you now have the whole picture: the column type decides which operators exist, and the operators decide which index earns its disk.

Originally published at https://andresleiva.com on July 28, 2026.
